claims.claim_text: The indexed Harry X. Boosel is high-confidence matched to the Chicago federal employee who served in Army counterintelligence and OSS, but the printed identifier conflicts with the exact-name Army row.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The distinctive exact name, 1912 birth year, Chicago context, federal career, and documented CIC and OSS service align; the official Army file differs by one identifier digit.
claims.identity_match_assessment: Multiple distinctive identifiers support the match, while the number discrepancy prevents confirmed status.
claims.temporal_assessment: The institutional biography places federal employment before a four-year wartime interruption and documents CIC and OSS service.
claims.match_notes: The exact number printed by the OSS index belongs to Ernest F. Pilz in the Army file; the exact-name Boosel row differs by one digit and matches the independent biography. Both facts remain visible.

sources.excerpt_override: spent four years in the Army Counter Intelligence Corps and the Office of Strategic Services

claims.claim_text: Before entering the Army in June 1942, Harry X. Boosel worked for the United States government; he had begun that federal career as a file clerk in 1936.
claims.evidence_excerpt: long career with the U.S. Government, starting as a file clerk in 1936
claims.evidence_paraphrase: A biographical account describes federal employment from 1936 interrupted by wartime service; the Army file supplies the June 1942 entry date.
claims.identity_match_assessment: The distinctive exact name and corroborating wartime biography support a high-confidence match despite the index-number discrepancy.
claims.temporal_assessment: The federal career is strongly bounded before Army entry, but the agency and final job are not named.
claims.match_notes: Publish as unspecified federal service, not as a named agency and not as his immediate OSS predecessor.

claims.claim_text: The high-confidence Harry X. Boosel Army row records civilian-occupation code 776, inspectors, not elsewhere classified, at Army entry.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The exact-name Army row carries occupation code 776; the official code list defines it as inspectors, n.e.c.
claims.identity_match_assessment: The row is a high-confidence match but differs by one identifier digit from the OSS index.
claims.temporal_assessment: The code describes civilian occupation at Army entry on June 15, 1942; it does not establish an employer or OSS accession date.
claims.match_notes: Occupation only. Do not infer the employing federal agency or equate inspector with the 1936 file-clerk starting role.

claims.claim_text: The indexed George A. Bopp is high-confidence matched to an Army entry record with the exact name, compatible chronology and rank progression, and a near-matching identifier.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The best Army candidate entered as a private in October 1942, was born in 1919, and differs from the printed OSS identifier by one omitted internal digit.
claims.identity_match_assessment: Exact name, near identifier, pre-OSS timing, and possible private-to-staff-sergeant progression support high confidence; the discrepancy prevents confirmation.
claims.temporal_assessment: The Army row predates the indexed OSS file, but the Army-to-OSS transfer date is unknown.
claims.match_notes: A second exact-name Army record from November 1945 has a different complete identifier and incompatible timing and was rejected.

claims.claim_text: The high-confidence George A. Bopp Army row records civilian-occupation code 242, attendants in hospitals and other institutions, not elsewhere classified.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The best Army row carries occupation code 242; the official code list defines a broad service-occupation group.
claims.identity_match_assessment: The near-identifier match is high confidence but not confirmed.
claims.temporal_assessment: The code describes civilian occupation at Army entry on October 12, 1942; it does not name an institution or prove immediacy to OSS.
claims.match_notes: No hospital, institution, employer, or specific job is inferred from the code.

claims.claim_text: The indexed Lieutenant Colonel Waller B. Booth Jr. is high-confidence matched to the uncommon-name OSS officer documented in official CIA and National Park Service histories.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: Official histories independently identify Waller Booth as a former OSS officer in Puerto Rico and an OSS operative in Tangier in late 1942.
claims.identity_match_assessment: The exact uncommon name, officer status, Puerto Rico context, and multiple OSS references distinguish him from namesakes.
claims.temporal_assessment: The official sources establish wartime OSS service; a family manuscript narrative supplies the earlier chronology.
claims.match_notes: Box 69 should still confirm the indexed private identifier and detailed assignment sequence.

claims.claim_text: Immediately before OSS, Waller B. Booth Jr. served in its institutional predecessor, the Coordinator of Information, beginning in December 1941.
claims.evidence_excerpt: In December, 1941, he had joined an organization called the Coordinator of Information
claims.evidence_paraphrase: A family narrative based on Booth's manuscript dates his volunteering to November 1941 and COI entry to December 1941.
claims.identity_match_assessment: Official CIA and NPS histories support the uncommon-name OSS identity; the narrative supplies the COI chronology.
claims.temporal_assessment: COI is explicitly the institutional predecessor immediately before OSS, not a civilian employer.
claims.match_notes: Qualified pending personnel-file corroboration of entry date and assignment title.

claims.claim_text: Before volunteering for the Coordinator of Information, Waller B. Booth Jr. co-owned and managed an unnamed bottling company in Puerto Rico.
claims.evidence_excerpt: with a family friend, he purchased a bottling company
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The family manuscript narrative places the unnamed Puerto Rico business after Booth left London in 1939 and before his November 1941 volunteering.
claims.identity_match_assessment: The narrative concerns the same uncommon-name OSS officer corroborated by official histories.
claims.temporal_assessment: This is the latest described civilian work before COI, strongly bounded but not independently corroborated.
claims.match_notes: The company remains unnamed; no business identity is guessed or normalized.

claims.claim_text: In the late 1930s, Waller B. Booth Jr. managed the London office of Raymond and Whitcomb Travel Company.
claims.evidence_excerpt: manager for the Raymond and Whitcomb Travel Company in London
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The family manuscript narrative documents Booth's London travel-company management before his return to the United States after war began in 1939.
claims.identity_match_assessment: The narrative concerns the same uncommon-name OSS officer corroborated by official histories.
claims.temporal_assessment: Definitely pre-OSS but not immediate because the Puerto Rico business intervened.
claims.match_notes: Earlier documented employment; it is not promoted to immediate or last-civilian status.

claims.claim_text: The indexed French Second Lieutenant Lucien H. Boquet is high-confidence matched to resistance agent and radio operator Lucien Boquet, alias Lucien Berlioz.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: An official French finding aid lists Lucien Boquet's individual resistance-agent dossier; a referenced research table places that rare name in OSS-related Mission Sanctuaire.
claims.identity_match_assessment: The rare exact name, French wartime status, officer context, and archival mission references support high confidence; the middle initial is not independently confirmed.
claims.temporal_assessment: Sources establish wartime resistance and OSS-related activity, not a pre-OSS employer or immediately prior assignment.
claims.match_notes: Alias Berlioz and occasional spelling Bocquet are search variants, not silent corrections. Review both French files and Box 69 before adding pre-OSS affiliations.
